content: Patient care teams are defined as groups of healthcare professionals from various disciplines who collaborate to provide comprehensive care for patients. These teams are typically organized under the leadership of a physician, with each team member assigned specific responsibilities. Together, the team works collectively to address the healthcare needs of the patient. The rationale for implementing multidisciplinary patient care teams in diabetes management is supported by the complexity and diversity of quality care markers required for diabetic patients. At a minimum, these markers include achieving glycemic control, blood pressure control, and lipid control. Additional indicators of quality care encompass smoking cessation, regular eye and dental examinations, foot examinations, vaccinations, and renal monitoring for albuminuria. In a randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of patient care teams in an international cohort of patients with poor cardiometabolic profiles (defined as glycated hemoglobin [HbA1c] levels ≥8%, systolic blood pressure ≥140 mm Hg, and/or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C] levels ≥130 mg/dL), only 2% of patients achieved comprehensive control of glycemic levels, blood pressure, and LDL-C goals. Comprehensive control was defined as achieving an HbA1c level of less than 7%, blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg, and LDL-C levels under 100 mg/dL. This rate of success was lower than that observed in a prior study conducted by Kaiser. The impact of patient care teams, along with other quality improvement initiatives aimed at enhancing diabetes care, has been systematically reviewed to assess their effectiveness in improving outcomes for diabetic patients.
